web_evidence.title: Extract | The Correspondent by Virginia Evans
web_evidence.note: The publisher’s sustained interior extract consists of a letter in which Sybil repeatedly narrates her accident, fears, and impending blindness as “I”; the page also describes the story as told through her letters.

web_evidence.title: The Correspondent Excerpt: Read free excerpt of The Correspondent by Virginia Evans
web_evidence.note: This Crown-authorized opening excerpt presents consecutive letters signed by Sybil, with sustained first-person accounts of her birthday, family history, and car accident.

web_evidence.title: To the Letter: A Conversation with Virginia Evans
web_evidence.note: The structural analysis and author interview state that, aside from a brief preface, the entire novel is composed of letters; nearly every letter is written by or to Sybil, and Evans explains that Sybil’s sent and received letters tell her life through participating correspondents.

web_evidence.title: Virginia Evans talks about the surprise hit novel ‘The Correspondent’
web_evidence.note: In this author interview, Evans confirms that the book is a series of emails and letters and discusses writing its first letter and building the characters’ world through that epistolary structure.

web_evidence.title: The Correspondent by Virginia Evans
web_evidence.note: The publisher describes Sybil’s lifelong use of letters to understand her own life and says the novel reveals one woman’s life one letter at a time, corroborating the epistolary participating voice.

person_note: The novel’s controlling narration is epistolary: Sybil and, at times, her correspondents participate in the story while writing as first-person letter voices. The quote set repeatedly exposes this constitutive “I/we” narration, and both authorized excerpts independently demonstrate it in sustained prose. Whole-book structural research confirms that nearly the entire novel consists of letters written by or to Sybil. Direct speech, externally attributed quotations, generic aphorisms, and recipient-addressing “you” passages were not treated as changes of narrative person. A brief prefatory frame is reported, but it is not a sustained competing narrative section; no source indicates second-person or sustained third-person alternation. The remaining uncertainty is limited to which correspondent authored isolated clipped quotes, not to the book’s controlling first-person mode.
